description:
Fully Locked In is a solo team led by Sweety Das, here to learn, build, and push through every hour of the hackathon.
One person, full focus, and a commitment to ship something real by the final buzzer.
summary: AstroVitals is a health self-monitoring app for astronauts on long missions. Far from Earth, astronauts must notice health changes in themselves, but they are not doctors. AstroVitals lets them log daily readings like heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood, exercise and food in a few minutes. It shows their health at a glance on a clickable human body, where each organ glows green, orange or red. Every warning explains what it means, what to do next, and when to contact the flight surgeon. An AI check learns each astronaut's normal and flags unusual readings early. A Flight Surgeon Report sums up the week for the medical team on Earth. The app covers NASA's 5 hazards of spaceflight and the problems they cause, like bone loss, immune changes and stress. This matters because on a Mars mission, help from Earth can take up to 20 minutes each way, so astronauts need to catch problems before they become emergencies.
details:
What it does

AstroVitals helps astronauts check their own health during long missions and know what to do next.

- Daily check-in (about 5 minutes): heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep, mood, exercise minutes and food energy, plus symptoms (like space sickness, headache, back pain or vision changes), a note, and an optional photo from the camera or an upload. Every reading has simple "how to measure" steps.

- Clickable body map: a realistic human body where each organ glows green, orange or red based on its health. Tapping a body part shows what it does, how space affects it, and its readings.

- Clear next steps: every warning explains what to do and when to contact the crew or the flight surgeon.

- AI anomaly detection: the app learns each astronaut's own normal from their first 14 days and flags readings that are unusual for them. A second model (Isolation Forest) looks at all readings together to catch risky combinations, like a fever with a high heart rate.

- Trends: charts show how each reading changes over the mission, with the normal range shaded.

- Flight Surgeon Report: a summary of the last 7 days, 14 days or the whole mission, with readings that need review, AI flags, symptoms and averages. It downloads as a report and raw data to send at the next communication window.

- Prevention: a daily tip for the body system that struggled most that week, a daily health routine, and a "check-in due" reminder.

- Mission environments: Space Station, Lunar Base, Lunar Rover Expedition, Mars Transit and Mars Surface, each with its gravity level and an estimated radiation dose compared with NASA's career limit.

- Health Guide: NASA's 5 hazards and every health reading explained in plain language.

Benefits and intended impact

On a Mars mission, messages to Earth can take up to about 20 minutes each way, so the crew must handle health problems mostly on their own. AstroVitals helps astronauts spot changes early, before they become emergencies, and gives the medical team on Earth a clear picture when they talk. It supports the flight surgeon and does not replace them. The same idea could also help people in remote places on Earth, like research stations or northern communities.

How it is creative

Instead of a plain list of numbers, health is shown on a realistic human body where each organ glows by its status and can be tapped to learn what it does and how space affects it. The AI check compares each astronaut with their own normal, not just general ranges. We chose practical tools over points and badges, like a report the flight surgeon actually reads.

Factors we considered

Astronauts are not doctors, so every reading has simple steps and plain-language advice. Long missions are stressful, so we used a calm, light colour palette. Communication delays mean the crew must act alone, so the app always says when a result needs the flight surgeon. The demo uses simulated data for 2 astronauts over a 90-day mission, with realistic events like space sickness, an isolation slump, a fever and a blood-pressure spike.

Tools used

Python, Streamlit, Plotly, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, SciPy and Pillow. Body illustration and logo made in Canva. SI (Claude by Anthropic) was used for guidance.
